title: The frontiers of mathematics
scope: Selected historical milestones; not an exhaustive current-record database.

problems.name: Twin prime gaps
problems.metric: Selected upper bound on recurring prime gaps
problems.question: Are there infinitely many prime pairs just two apart?
problems.explanation: Prime pairs such as 11 and 13, or 17 and 19, differ by 2. The twin-prime conjecture says there are infinitely many such pairs.
problems.chartDescription: Selected upper bounds on the limit inferior of consecutive prime gaps, on a logarithmic scale.
problems.chartNote: H₁ is the limit inferior of consecutive prime gaps. A bound means infinitely many pairs are at least this close, not that all gaps are this small. Dates use public reports.
problems.interpretation: The published bound fell from 70 million to 246 in just over a year. The conjecture asks for a gap of 2. The reported 186 result has a conditional Lean formalization, not a complete formal proof.
problems.note: An independent August 31, 2026 preprint by Julia Stadlmann gives 240. It is not another step here: the 186 manuscript is dated August 30. These are manuscript dates, not a priority judgment.

milestones.label: May 2013
milestones.title: The first finite bound
milestones.detail: Zhang proved that infinitely many consecutive prime pairs have a gap below 70 million. Accepted in May 2013; published in Annals of Mathematics in 2014.

milestones.label: Sep 2013
milestones.title: Polymath reduces the bound to 4,680
milestones.detail: A worldwide collaboration rapidly reduced the bound. Tao’s September 2013 account records 4,680; the paper followed in 2014.

milestones.label: Nov 2013
milestones.who: James Maynard; method independently developed by Terence Tao
milestones.title: Maynard’s sieve gives 600
milestones.detail: Maynard’s preprint gives a bound of 600 with a different sieve method. Published in Annals of Mathematics in 2015.

milestones.label: Jul 2014
milestones.title: Polymath reduces the bound to 246
milestones.detail: The collaboration refined the new method and proved the unconditional bound 246. Published in Research in the Mathematical Sciences in 2014.

milestones.label: Aug 2026
milestones.title: A reported bound of 186
milestones.detail: The manuscript claims an unconditional mathematical bound of 186. Its Lean formalization assumes three input axioms, covering exponential-sum estimates and numerical bounds. The repository makes these dependencies explicit.
milestones.ai: The paper credits GPT-6 Astra with the proof. The Lean development remains conditional on input axioms; numerical checks use Python/FLINT.

problems.name: Riemann zeros
problems.metric: Selected lower bound on the critical-line proportion
problems.question: Do all nontrivial zeta zeros lie on one line?
problems.explanation: The Riemann hypothesis places every nontrivial zero on the line with real part ½. One approach proves that an increasing proportion must lie there.
problems.unit: Asymptotic proportion on the critical line
problems.chartDescription: Selected proven lower bounds on the asymptotic proportion of zeta zeros on the critical line.
problems.chartNote: This is an asymptotic lower density, not a count of zeros checked by a computer. Earlier published results are plotted at their public or publication year.
problems.interpretation: Even a proven proportion of 100% would not by itself prove the Riemann hypothesis: a zero-density set of exceptions could remain. This chart is not a percentage solved.
problems.note: An independent September 2026 preprint by Youness Lamzouri gives a simpler proof of the same 67.25% bound. It adds evidence, not another upward step. This is a selected history, not an exhaustive ledger of every recent claim.

milestones.title: Levinson’s 34.74% bound
milestones.detail: Levinson proved that more than one third of the zeros lie on the critical line. The numerical 34.74% version is documented in the Bui–Conrey–Young paper’s historical introduction.

milestones.title: Conrey’s 40.88% bound
milestones.detail: Conrey’s published result increased the lower bound to more than 40.88%. The numerical value is documented in the Pratt–Robles–Zaharescu–Zeindler introduction.

milestones.who: Hung Bui, Brian Conrey, Matthew Young
milestones.title: A lower bound of 41.05%
milestones.detail: Theorem 1.1 establishes a lower bound of 41.05%. First posted in 2010 and published in Acta Arithmetica in 2011.

milestones.who: Kyle Pratt, Nicolas Robles, Alexandru Zaharescu, Dirk Zeindler
milestones.title: A lower bound of 41.7293%
milestones.detail: The paper’s refined numerical bound is 41.7293%, slightly better than five twelfths. The preprint appeared in 2018; publication followed in 2020.

milestones.title: A reported lower bound of 67.25%
milestones.detail: The preprint proves a lower bound of 67.25% for zeros that are both simple and on the critical line. The authors say they verified the argument and take responsibility for it.
milestones.ai: The authors credit Claude with discovering and writing the argument. They checked it themselves; journal peer review is not established here.

problems.name: Matrix multiplication
problems.metric: Selected upper bound on the exponent ω
problems.question: How fast can we multiply two square matrices?
problems.explanation: The standard algorithm takes roughly n³ arithmetic operations. Faster algorithms reduce the exponent. The conjectured optimum is 2.
problems.chartDescription: Selected upper bounds on the matrix multiplication exponent, with conjectured target 2.
problems.chartNote: ω describes asymptotic field-operation complexity, not benchmarked runtime. The zoom view reveals recent improvements without moving the target.
problems.interpretation: The exponent has fallen by less than 0.002 since 1990. These asymptotic bounds describe performance as matrix sizes grow; they do not necessarily improve practical runtimes.

milestones.title: Strassen’s recursive algorithm
milestones.detail: Strassen broke the cubic barrier with a recursive algorithm, giving an exponent of log₂(7), approximately 2.807355.

milestones.title: The Coppersmith–Winograd bound
milestones.detail: The Coppersmith–Winograd method pushed the exponent below 2.376. This chart uses 2.375477 from Tao’s numerical reference ledger and the journal publication year, 1990; conference presentation was in 1987.

milestones.title: Le Gall’s tensor analysis
milestones.detail: New analysis gave an exponent below 2.3728639. Posted and published at ISSAC in 2014.

milestones.who: Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams
milestones.title: A refined laser method
milestones.detail: A stronger analysis lowered the exponent to 2.3728596. Preprint in 2020; SODA publication in 2021.

milestones.who: Ran Duan, Hongxun Wu, Renfei Zhou
milestones.title: Asymmetric hashing improves the bound
milestones.detail: The asymmetric hashing approach improved the exponent to below 2.371866. Preprint in 2022; FOCS publication in 2023.

milestones.who: Virginia Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu, Renfei Zhou
milestones.title: An upper bound of 2.371552
milestones.detail: The authors report an upper bound of 2.371552. Preprint in 2023; SODA publication in 2024.

milestones.who: Josh Alman, Ran Duan, Virginia Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu, Zixuan Xu, Renfei Zhou
milestones.title: An upper bound of 2.371339
milestones.detail: Further refinements yield an exponent below 2.371339. First posted in April 2024 and published at SODA in 2025.

milestones.title: AlphaEvolve-assisted optimization
milestones.detail: The preprint combines gradient optimization with an algorithm refined by AlphaEvolve. It reports an exponent below 2.371177 and rigorous verification of the resulting bound.
milestones.ai: AlphaEvolve refined the optimization algorithm after gradient-based optimization had already improved the existing bound. This is distinct from small-matrix records by AlphaTensor.

problems.name: Ramsey numbers
problems.metric: Possible values of R(5,5) in this snapshot
problems.question: How big a party guarantees a group of five?
problems.explanation: Assume acquaintance is mutual. How many guests guarantee five who all know one another—or five who are all strangers? That number is R(5,5).
problems.chartDescription: Upper and lower bounds on R(5,5). The upper bound descends from 53 to 46; the lower bound stays at 43.
problems.chartNote: The shaded band contains the possible integer answers. Lower bound 43 dates to Exoo’s 1989 construction; this selected series begins in 1992.
problems.interpretation: The answer is one of 43, 44, 45, or 46. The lower bound has stood since 1989. Almost all the narrowing shown here comes from above.

milestones.who: Brendan McKay and Stanisław Radziszowski; lower bound by Geoffrey Exoo
milestones.title: Eleven possible answers
milestones.detail: The range is 43 through 53, inclusive. The authors’ later presentation records the 1992 upper bound and the subsequent improvements.

milestones.title: One more possibility eliminated
milestones.detail: The upper bound falls to 52. Historical date and value are recorded in McKay and Angeltveit’s 2017 presentation.

milestones.title: Below fifty-one
milestones.detail: The upper bound falls to 50, leaving eight possible integer answers. Historical date and value follow the authors’ presentation.

milestones.title: A bound that holds for twenty years
milestones.detail: The upper bound reaches 49. The next improvement in this selected history does not arrive until 2017.

milestones.title: Six possible answers remain
milestones.detail: The authors prove R(5,5) ≤ 48 with computer-assisted methods. The preprint appeared in 2017 and was published in 2018.

milestones.title: Down to four integers
milestones.detail: Mathematics, linear programming and extensive computation establish R(5,5) ≤ 46. The authors report independent replication. Preprint in 2024; journal publication in 2026.

problems.name: Odd perfect numbers
problems.metric: Selected lower bound on an odd perfect number
problems.question: Can a perfect number be odd?
problems.explanation: 6 is perfect: its proper positive divisors, 1, 2 and 3, add up to 6. Every known perfect number is even. Any odd perfect number must exceed the lower bounds shown here.
problems.chartDescription: Published lower bounds on the size of an odd perfect number, followed by an unpublished 2014 report. Vertical values are powers of ten.
problems.chartNote: The vertical axis plots the exponent: 1,500 means 10^1500. Dates are publication years, except the 2014 author presentation. The undated 10^2200 extension is not plotted.
problems.interpretation: Ruling out every candidate below 10^1500 still leaves infinitely many larger candidates. A growing exclusion bound does not tell us whether an odd perfect number exists.
problems.note: Pascal Ochem’s institutional project page now reports a bound of 10^2200. Its announcement date was not verified, so it is not assigned a 2026 position on this timeline.

milestones.title: A lower bound of 10²⁰
milestones.detail: Kanold’s 1957 lower bound of 10^20 is recorded in the introduction to Hagis’s original 1973 paper. This milestone is sourced through that later mathematical paper.

milestones.title: A lower bound of 10⁵⁰
milestones.detail: Hagis proves that an odd perfect number must exceed 10^50. The date is the publication year; this selected timeline omits some intermediate bounds.

milestones.title: A lower bound of 10¹⁶⁰
milestones.detail: The published paper raises the lower bound to 10^160 using restrictions on the prime factors of an odd perfect number.

milestones.who: Richard Brent, Graeme Cohen, Herman te Riele
milestones.title: A lower bound of 10³⁰⁰
milestones.detail: The journal paper proves the 10^300 lower bound. A full technical report had already appeared in October 1989; this chart consistently uses the publication year.

milestones.title: The published bound reaches 10¹⁵⁰⁰
milestones.detail: A computer-assisted proof establishes that any odd perfect number exceeds 10^1500. Published in Mathematics of Computation in 2012.

milestones.title: An unpublished bound of 10²⁰⁰⁰
milestones.detail: The authors’ dated Montpellier presentation reports 10^2000 and explicitly labels the extension unpublished. It is displayed as an author report, separately from the published bound.

problems.name: Hadamard matrices
problems.metric: Unresolved orders through 2,000 in this snapshot
problems.question: Can every multiple of four make a perfect ±1 grid?
problems.explanation: A Hadamard matrix has entries +1 or −1 and mutually perpendicular rows. The conjecture asks for one at every positive order divisible by four.
problems.chartDescription: A grid of 500 orders divisible by four, from 4 to 2000. Published snapshots leave 13, then 12 gaps; 2026 constructions are reported for the remaining 12.
problems.chartNote: Only orders divisible by four, from 4 to 2,000, are shown. Hatched cells are reported constructions, not unresolved cases. The general conjecture concerns infinitely many orders.
problems.interpretation: Filling every gap through 2,000 would settle a finite collection of cases. It would not prove the Hadamard conjecture for all multiples of four.
problems.note: The independent August 13, 2026 check by Ion Nechita covers order 668. Epoch reports all 12 constructions; this collection has not independently checked every matrix. AI attribution on Epoch’s page is provisional.

milestones.title: Thirteen gaps below 2,000
milestones.detail: A construction of order 764 leaves the 13 orders listed in the paper’s introduction unresolved through 2,000. The original list gives each order divided by four.

milestones.who: Dragomir Ž. Đoković, Oleg Golubitsky, Ilias S. Kotsireas
milestones.title: Order 1,004 is filled in
milestones.detail: The paper constructs order 1,004 and lists the remaining 12 gaps. Preprint in January 2013; journal publication in 2014.

milestones.label: Aug 2026
milestones.who: Levent Alpöge and collaborators; Claude contribution reported by Epoch
milestones.title: Constructions reported for the remaining twelve
milestones.detail: Epoch’s problem page records constructions for all previously unknown admissible orders through 2,000. Ion Nechita independently checked the matrix of order 668; this is not a proof of the general conjecture.
milestones.ai: Epoch credits three human researchers working with an internal Claude model and explicitly marks the AI attribution provisional.
